source_text: Πῶς οὖν καὶ τοῦτο ἐξεπορίσθη; κηδεστὴν μου ἄνδρα ἀδελφῆς ἐμῆς, ὁ τότε ἄρχων τῶν Παλαιστινῶν, τοῦτον παραλαβὼν ἐξαίφνης ἄκοντα μόνον κεχωρισμένον τῆς ὁμοζύγου, ἦγεν ἐνταῦθα, συνεπιβοηθήσοντα καὶ κοινωνήσοντα τῶν τοῦ ἔθνους ἀρχικῶν πόνων. νομικὸς γάρ τις ἦν, καὶ ἔστιν ἴσως ἔτι. ὃς δὴ ἐλθὼν ἅμα αὐτῷ, ἔμελλε μὲν οὐκ εἰς μακρὰν μεταπεμψάμενος ἀπολήψεσθαι τὴν γυναῖκα, ἐπαχθῶς αὐτῆς καὶ ἄκων κεχωρισμένος, καὶ ἡμᾶς δὲ ἅμα αὐτῇ συνεπισπώμενος. ἐξαίφνης γοῦν, οὐκ οἶδ᾽ ὅπως ἀποδημεῖν μὲν, ἀλλ᾽ ἑτέρωθί ποι μᾶλλον ἀποδημεῖν ἢ ἐνταῦθα διανοουμένοις ἡμῖν, ἐπέστη στρατιώτης φέρων ἐντολὴν, παραπέμπειν μὲν καὶ διασώζεσθαι τὴν ἀδελφὴν ἡμῶν καταλαμβάνουσαν τὸν ἄνδρα, ἄγειν δὲ καὶ ἡμᾶς συνοδοιπόρους ἅμ᾽ αὐτῇ. χαριουμένους μὲν καὶ τῷ κηδεστῇ, καὶ μάλιστα τῇ ἀδελφῇ· ὅπως μὴ οὐκ εὐσχήμων τι ἢ ὀκνηροτέρα πρὸς τὴν ὁδοιπορίαν, ἢ, οἰκέταις αὖθις καὶ τοῖς συγγενέσι τιμήσασι, καὶ οὐ μικρόν τι ἕτερον τῶν προὔργου διαπραξαμένοις, εἰ ἐπὶ τὴν Βηρυτίων ἔλθοιμεν πόλιν, ἐκεῖ τὸ τῶν νόμων μάθημα ἐκπονήσοντες. πάντα τοιγαροῦν ἐκίνει ἡμᾶς τὸ πρὸς τὴν ἀδελφὴν εὔλογον, τὸ ἡμέτερον αὐτῶν μάθημα· πρὸς δὲ, καὶ ὁ στρατιώτης, ἐπεὶ καὶ τούτου μνημονεῦσαι δεῖ, φέρων ἐξουσίαν πλειόνων τῶν δημοσίων ὀχημάτων τῆς χρήσεως, καὶ σύμβολα πλείονος ἀριθμοῦ ἡμῶν μᾶλλον, ἢ τῆς ἀδελφῆς μόνης ἕνεκα. φαινόμενα μὲν ταῦτα, τὰ δὲ μὴ φαινόμενα μὲν, ἀληθέστερα δὲ, ἡ πρὸς τὸν ἄνδρα τόνδε κοινωνία, ἡ ἀληθὴς δι᾽ αὐτοῦ περὶ τὰ τοῦ λόγου μαθήματα, ἡ τῶν ψυχῶν ἡμῶν ὠφέλεια, εἰς σωτηρίαν ἦγεν ἡμᾶς, ἔπειτα δὲ τυφλώττοντας μὲν καὶ οὐκ εἰδότας, σωτηριωδῶς δὲ ἡμῖν. τοιγαροῦν οὐχ ὁ στρατιώτης, θεῖος δέ τις συνοδοιπόρος καὶ πομπὸς ἀγαθὸς καὶ φύλαξ, ὁ διὰ παντὸς τοῦ βίου τούτου, ὥσπερ μακρᾶς ὁδοιπορίας διασώζων ἡμᾶς, παραμειψάμενος τά τε ἄλλα, καὶ τὴν Βηρυτὸν, ἧς μάλιστα ὁρμᾶν ἐνταῦθα ᾠήθημεν, ἐνταῦθα φέρων κατέστησε, πάντα ποιῶν καὶ κινῶν, ἕως πάσῃ μηχανῇ τῷ τῶν πολλῶν ἡμῖν ἀγαθῶν αἰτίῳ τούτῳ συνδήσειε. καὶ ὁ μὲν, διὰ τοσούτων ἐλθὼν τὴν οἰκονομίαν παραδιδοὺς τούτῳ ὁ θεῖος ἄγγελος, ἐνταῦθά που καὶ ἴσως ἀνεπαύσατο, οὐχ ὑπὸ καμάτου τινὸς ἢ μόχθου. (ἀκάματον γὰρ τὸ τῶν θείων λειτουργῶν γένος.) ἀλλ᾽ ὅτι παρέδωκεν ἀνθρώπῳ, πᾶσαν, εἰ δυνατὸν, πρόνοιαν καὶ ἐπιμέλειαν ἀποπληρώσοντι.
thought_title: The soldier, the journey, and the angel's handing over
orientation: A soldier sent to escort his sister brings Gregory to Caesarea, where his guardian angel hands him over to Origen.
pass_a_gloss: How then was this too provided (exeporisthe)? My brother-in-law (kedestes), the husband of my sister: the then ruler (archon) of the Palestinians, taking him suddenly, unwilling, separated alone from his spouse (homozygos), was bringing him here, to help together and share in the governing labors (archikoi ponoi) of the province (ethnos). For he was a lawyer (nomikos), and perhaps still is. Who, having come with him, was about before long, having sent for her, to receive back the wife, being separated from her grievously (epachthos) and unwillingly, and to draw us along together with her. Suddenly then, while we, I know not how, were intending to go abroad, but rather somewhere elsewhere than here, there stood by (epeste) a soldier (stratiotes) bearing an order (entole): to escort and keep safe our sister as she joined her husband, and to bring us also as fellow travelers (synodoiporoi) with her; as going to do a favor (charioumenous) to the brother-in-law, and most of all to the sister, so that [she] not [go] unbecomingly (euschemon) or more hesitant (oknerotera) toward the journey; or, to the household (oiketai) again and the relatives (syngeneis) who valued [it] and accomplished no small other thing of the profitable (proergou), if we should come to the city of the Berytians, there to work through (ekponesontes) the study (mathema) of the laws. Therefore all things moved us: what was reasonable (eulogon) toward the sister (pros ten adelphen), our own study; and besides, the soldier too, since he too must be mentioned, bearing authority (exousia) for the use of more of the public vehicles (ochemata), and tokens (symbola) of a larger number, for our sake rather than for the sister alone. These were the appearing things (phainomena); but the not appearing and truer things: the fellowship (koinonia) with this man, the true [instruction] through him in the lessons (mathemata) of the Word (logos), the benefit (opheleia) of our souls, were leading us to salvation (soteria), then being blind (typhlottontas) and not knowing, but savingly (soteriodos) for us. Therefore not the soldier, but some divine fellow traveler and good escort (pompos) and guardian (phylax), who through the whole (dia pantos) of this life, as of a long journey, keeps us safe, having passed by both the other things and Berytus, where we thought most of all to be setting out, bringing [us] here, settled [us], doing and moving all things, until by every device (mechane) he bound us together with this man, the cause (aitios) of our many goods. And he, having come through so many [things], handing over the dispensation/charge (oikonomia) to this man, the divine angel (angelos), here somewhere perhaps rested (anepausato), not under any weariness (kamatos) or toil (mochthos) (for the race of divine ministers (leitourgoi) is unwearied (akamatos)), but because he handed over to a man who would fulfill (apoplerosonti), if possible, all forethought (pronoia) and care (epimeleia).

pass_b_english: How, then, was this too provided? My brother-in-law, my sister's husband, was taken up suddenly by the man who was then governor of Palestine and brought here against his will, parted from his wife and alone, to help him and share the labors of governing the province. For he was a lawyer, and perhaps still is. Having come with the governor, he meant before long to send for his wife and have her with him again, since he was parted from her unwillingly and with distress, and to draw us along with her. Then suddenly, I do not know how, while we were planning to travel, though to some other place rather than here, a soldier appeared with orders to escort our sister and see her safely to her husband, and to bring us too as her fellow travelers. We would be doing a kindness to our brother-in-law, and most of all to our sister, so that she would not make the journey in any unseemly way or with greater reluctance; and to our household and kin as well, who valued the plan and held that no small further gain would come of it if we went to the city of Berytus to work through our study of law there.

So everything moved us: what was fitting toward our sister, our own studies, and besides these the soldier as well (for he too must be mentioned), who carried authority to use a larger number of the public carriages, and passes for more people, for our sake rather than for our sister's alone. These were the visible reasons. But the hidden and truer ones were these: fellowship with this man, the true teaching of the Word that would come through him, the good of our souls. These were leading us toward salvation, while we were then still blind and unknowing, yet in a way that would save us.

So it was not the soldier, but a divine fellow traveler, a good escort and guardian, who keeps us safe through the whole of this life, as on a long journey. He passed by other places, and Berytus too, where we had thought we were chiefly heading, and brought us here and settled us, doing everything and setting everything in motion, until by every means he had bound us to this man, the cause of so many blessings for us. And so this divine angel, having come through so much and handing over his charge to this man, perhaps rested here, not from any weariness or toil (for the race of divine ministers never tires), but because he had handed it over to a man who would supply, as far as that was possible, all forethought and care.
notes: The opening sentence is an anacoluthon in the print (the governor's name stands as a hanging subject); it is smoothed into one English clause. The datives 'oiketais authis kai tois syngenesi timesasi ... diapraxamenois' were read from damaged line ends and do not construe cleanly; the English follows their plain sense, matched by the Latin column ('domesticis ipsis et cognatis hortantibus, et non exiguum aliud quoddam operaepretium fore contendentibus'). 'What was fitting toward our sister': the 1622 print reads 'to pros t[en] adelphen' at the foot of p. 57 and 'eulogon' at the head of p. 58 (PDF pp. 81-82, checked on the page images). Koetschau and the Latin ('erga sororem officium') agree. 'A larger number of the public carriages' (Greek pleionon ton demosion ochematon); the Latin adds 'than was needed'. 'Then' in 'blind and unknowing as we then were' renders the print's epeita (Latin has no matching word). 'The true teaching of the Word': the Greek noun after he alethes is not expressed; logos here can mean reason as well as the divine Word (Latin 'vera verbi ... cognitio et doctrina'). 'Where we had thought we were chiefly heading': the print reads entautha twice; the first is probably an error for ekeise (thither) and is not translated as 'here'. 'Who keeps us safe through the whole of this life': the print reads 'ho dia pantos tou biou toutou' (PDF p. 82; Latin 'qui per totam hanc vitam'). 'Handing over his charge to this man': the print reads 'ten oikonomian paradidous toutoi' (PDF p. 82). The divine fellow traveler is the guardian angel of 4.2, so 'escort' and 'guardian' stay lowercase. Allusions left uncited: the angel as fellow traveler may recall Raphael with Tobias (Tobit 5), and 'divine ministers' (leitourgoi) may echo the 'ministering spirits' of Hebrews 1:14; neither is quoted.
